disease_info: Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features is characterized by one or more major depressive episodes accompanied by delusions and/or hallucinations that occur exclusively during these depressive episodes. The psychotic content is often mood-congruent, involving themes of guilt, worthlessness, illness, or deserved punishment, and is typically less systematized than in primary psychotic disorders. Clinically, it tends to present with more severe functional impairment, higher suicide risk, and greater psychomotor and cognitive slowing than non-psychotic depression, and may have a recurrent course. It is distinguished from schizoaffective disorder and schizophrenia by the absence of psychotic symptoms outside of mood episodes and by the temporal alignment between mood disturbance and psychosis.

narrative.personality: Aaron is a warm, routine-loving caregiver who thrives on community connections and simple pleasures but can be laid-back and disorganized about his own obligations.
narrative.stressor: Over the past year, Aaron’s hours at the home-care agency were repeatedly cut as several long-term clients were moved to assisted living, leaving him juggling part-time shifts at different sites and falling behind on rent and bills. His easygoing attitude toward paperwork and money, which had never caused more than minor hassles before, suddenly led to overdraft fees, collection calls, and the real possibility of eviction, which he experienced as a humiliating failure given his reputation as a dependable aide and church volunteer. As the financial pressure mounted, he began skipping social activities and fishing trips to take every available shift, yet still watched his debts grow, and he grew increasingly withdrawn and preoccupied with the idea that he was being judged and quietly talked about by neighbors and coworkers. After about two months of this decline, he finally came to psychiatric care at the urging of his pastor and a supervisor, who were alarmed by his dramatic weight loss, inability to keep up with simple tasks, and his insistence that his financial problems were a sign that God and the community had turned against him.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve dropped so much weight without trying, and I just don’t feel like eating anymore.”

narrative.personality: Galina is an energetic, art-obsessed organizer with a competitive drive and sociable flair who delights in cultural events, learning, and playful mischief in the kitchen.
narrative.stressor: About three months before presentation, Galina’s closest friend and long-time co-organizer at the arts center died suddenly after a brief illness, a loss that shattered both her daily routine and her primary emotional support. The pair had shared nearly every project, from grant proposals to museum tours to late-night jazz outings, and Galina felt abruptly alone in both her personal life and her community work, questioning the point of continuing their ambitious plans. In the weeks following the funeral, she threw herself into organizing a memorial exhibit but became increasingly unsettled by the feeling that she was somehow responsible for missing signs of her friend’s illness, and she started spending long, sleepless nights replaying their last conversations and searching for “proof” of her failures. As her exhaustion deepened and she began voicing increasingly fixed and implausible ideas that her friend’s death was a punishment for her own selfishness, her book club and fellow docents urged her to see a psychiatrist, concerned by her marked deterioration in functioning and her inability to rest or take care of herself.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I just can’t sleep anymore, no matter how tired I am.”

narrative.personality: Maria is a calm, collaborative healthcare leader who enjoys learning, gardening, and cooking, and prefers flexible structure even though she can be casually disorganized.
narrative.stressor: Six months before seeking help, Maria was promoted to lead a major system-wide quality initiative that came with intense scrutiny from senior leadership and tight performance benchmarks, on top of ongoing staffing shortages in her region. Initially she approached the challenge with her usual curiosity and confidence, but the constant stream of emails, late meetings, and budget constraints began to erode her sense of control, especially as she felt caught between executive demands and exhausted frontline staff. Over the following two months she gradually withdrew from the activities that had grounded her—skipping yoga, letting her garden go untended, and turning down family hikes—while becoming increasingly absorbed in ruminations that she had already irreparably damaged patient care and that colleagues were quietly compiling evidence of her incompetence. When her spouse noticed that she stopped engaging in even her beloved weekend cooking and began expressing fixed, self-blaming ideas about being responsible for systemic failures well beyond her role, they persuaded her to see a psychiatrist after she started missing work and could no longer manage basic decisions at home.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I don’t enjoy any of the things I used to love doing anymore.”
